newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices drop as U.N. gives final OK to Iraq oil deal.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices drop as U.N. gives final OK to Iraq oil deal.

text.p: Crude oil prices fell Monday on news that the United Nations had given its final stamp of approval to a deal that would allow Iraq to start shipping oil for the first time since its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
January crude oil ended down 32 cents at $25.30 a barrel after falling as low as $25 on the New York Mercantile Exchange.

Benchmark Brent Blend crude from the North Sea for January delivery fell to $23.77 a barrel before recovering to close at $24.08 a barrel, down 46 cents, after U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali gave final approval to the partial Iraqi oil sales deal.
Crude oil prices remain around $3 a barrel higher than this time last year, largely because of the absence of some 3 million barrels of Iraqi crude oil.
Oil traders said the market's immediate reaction was psychological and they remained sceptical that any Iraqi oil woould be seen on the world market for several weeks.

"The Iraqis have been threatening us with their sword of Damocles for ages but we don't know if that sword is sharp. It may be plastic," said Charles Gray, senior vice president for investments at Prudential Bache in London.

Under the U.N. deal, Iraq will export its first oil since August 1990, when the United Nations reacted to the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait by slapping it with economic sanctions, including a ban on oil exports.

Under a May 20 agreement, Iraq will be allowed to export up to a total $2.0 billion worth of oil over six months to buy humanitarian goods, which it has been unable to import because it has been deprived of vital oil revenue.

Iraq, which prior to the U.N. sanctions ranked as the second biggest oil producer in the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries, produced 3.5 million barrels a day in July 1990. Saudi Arabia is the top OPEC producer.
A senior trader for a European oil company said the threat of resumed Iraqi exports had been weighing on the market for years and was already discounted.

At current prices, Iraq would be able to export no more than 650,000 barrels per day, which analysts say can easily be absorbed by a market that has been tight due to cold weather and low inventories of crude oil and heating oil.
